extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor, literary critics, and writers interested in comic theory
extracted.subtask_description: A close theoretical analysis of the mechanisms that produce the comic in actions, situations, and language; intended to classify and illustrate the forms (repetition, inversion, transposition, reciprocal interference, etc.) by which laughter is elicited. Uses literary examples to demonstrate each mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of two independent series
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic arises when two independently developing series of words/actions/episodes meet so that actions and words that belong to one might equally belong to the other, revealing a coincidence of independence and coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage-made misunderstandings are a particular (often artificial) instance: the author repeatedly threatens the dissolution of the partnership between the two series and then patches things up, producing 'diversion' that excites laughter. Example: placing Tartarin manacled to Bonivard's chain to make two independent stories appear to coincide. Labiche's plays often build series separately and then make them interfere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition (series reproduced under new circumstances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy often depends on repeating a set of actions or relations—either reproducing the same scene between the same characters under new circumstances or between new characters under the same circumstances—so life is presented as a repeating mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic comedy favours repetition (the favourite method). Example: servants repeating scenes of their masters in less dignified language. Repetition is one of the three ways a series may become comic (with inversion and reciprocal interference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inversion (reversal of series or sentence elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy may be produced by turning a series or sentence upside down while still leaving a certain meaning; in sentences this can be done by reversing roles (subject/object) or by other syntactic inversions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inversion is the least interesting of the three fundamental laws but commonly used by wits (e.g., 'What do you mean by emptying your pipe on to my terrace?' — 'What do you mean by putting your terrace under my pipe?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisation of life / absentmindedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective of light comedy is to obtain a 'mechanisation of life': treating life as a repeating mechanism with reversible action and interchangeable parts; ludicrousness in events is defined as 'absentmindedness in things.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This absentmindedness is exceptional in real life and is artificially exaggerated in comedy. Light comedy depends on this artificial exaggeration (a jointed dancing-doll analogy). As a result it is often a game depending on a previously accepted convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic in words vs. comic expressed (language-specific comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish the comic that can be translated ('comic expressed') from the comic created by language itself ('comic in words') which often cannot be translated because it owes its being to sentence structure or word choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The comic in words stresses lapses of attention in language itself; comic sayings can sometimes be detached from the speaker and still be funny. Translation may lose significance; many examples in one language (e.g., M. Prudhomme) do not carry over literally into another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as the comic in volatile form / method of analysing witty remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: A witty saying is the comic in a highly volatile state; to analyse a witty remark: enlarge it into a regular scene and determine the comic category to which that scene belongs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Your chest hurts me' (Mme. de Sévigné) enlarges into a Molière scene where the doctor diagnoses the daughter by feeling the father's pulse. Witty retorts are miniature comic scenes; wit often operates by making others say or imply the opposite of what they mean.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready-made phrase + absurd idea rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic meaning is invariably obtained when an absurd idea is fitted into a well-established phrase-form (i.e., an automatism of language revealed by an absurd insertion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Ce sabre est le plus beau jour de ma vie' — the absurdity fitted into the ready-made phrase-end makes the automatism obvious and comic. M. Prudhomme exemplifies a character whose habitual set phrases become comic when combined with absurd content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literalising figurative expressions (materialising metaphors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect is obtained whenever we pretend to take literally an expression which was used figuratively; fixing attention on the material/physical side of a metaphor makes the idea comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Tous les arts sont frères' becomes comic if attention is drawn to material relationship; 'Tous les arts sont sœurs' or gender mismatch increases comic tinge. Literal replies to figurative talk (e.g., 'He won't catch it' to 'running after a joke') can be witty when the rejoinder borrows concrete language so vivid that we visualize it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal interference of meanings in a sentence (pun vs play on words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises when a single sentence legitimately or seemingly expresses two independent sets of ideas—either via homophony (pun) or via multiple meanings of a word—so the meanings jostle one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pun is a 'less reputable' form (different sentences conflated by sound); more refined play upon words uses one sentence that genuinely accommodates two senses, producing a momentary lapse of language's normal function and hence amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transposition of expression into another key
rubrics_metrics.description: A comic effect is always obtainable by transposing the natural expression of an idea into another key (e.g., solemn into familiar, familiar into solemn, high register into low register).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes parody (solemn -> familiar), mock-heroic (exaggeration upward or downward), and many gradations. Example: describing dawn 'like a lobster being boiled' transposes poetic diction into the familiar and produces parody. Transposition is a broad, central device with many subforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody / degradation (solemn to trivial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transposing the solemn into the familiar creates parody; making something formerly dignified appear mean (degradation) is one form of comic transposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While some philosophers equate comic with degradation, the text cautions that degradation is only one form of transposition among many and not the ultimate source of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration (treating small as large; prolonged/systematic hyperbole)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration is comic when small matters are treated as very large or when systematic/prolonged exaggeration makes the treatment absurd; it is a form of transposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggeration gives rise to mock-heroic and braggadocio; it can be very striking especially when methodical. Example contexts: boasting, mock-heroic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uplifting transposition of moral value (treating low as respectable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Describing disreputable, low-class, or scandalous situations in the most respectable language (transposition upwards in moral key) is comic and often especially effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characteristic in English literature (Dickens, Thackeray). The effect can be achieved with a single word that reveals an entire accepted system of transposition, e.g., Gogol: 'Your peculations are too extensive for an official of your rank.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Language's momentary lapse / negligence as comic source
rubrics_metrics.description: The play upon words and other verbal comic effects betray a momentary lapse of attention in language—language momentarily forgetting its function and accommodating things to itself—this negligence is amusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This underlying idea explains why puns and other wordplays produce laughter: they expose a temporary failure in language's normal correspondence with thought and reality.
